title: From stable periodic orbits to many-body chaos: doubly tunable prethermalization via engineering of an emergent band structure
authors: Jianan Wang, Yang Hou, Andrea Pizzi, Johannes Knolle, Roderich Moessner, Hongzheng Zhao
abstract: We uncover a family of many-body periodic orbits in a periodically driven (Floquet) spin system away from the high-frequency limit. While linear stability analysis predicts that perturbed many-body trajectories remain close to stable periodic orbits, thermodynamic principles dictate that Floquet heating will ultimately set in. Our work aims to resolve the tension between these two expectations. In particular, we show that perturbations away from the stable periodic orbits feature a description akin to a quasiparticle band structure. A long-lived prethermal regime appears when modes around the gapless point are slowly populated. The dispersion determines the prethermal lifetime, and we show how band engineering leads to a "doubly tunable" parametric dependence of the prethermal lifetime $R^{-W}$, with $R$ the width in momentum space of the quasiparticle distribution and $W$ the exponent of the dispersion around the gapless point. Our results not only establish a powerful route toward stabilizing non-equilibrium phases of matter in driven many-body systems but also establish a conceptual bridge between periodic orbits in 'low-dimensional' nonlinear systems and many-body chaos.
summary: The authors investigate how periodically driven spin systems exhibit long-lived prethermalization before full thermalization. They show that by carefully engineering the system's emergent quasiparticle band structure using further-range interactions, they can achieve a 'doubly tunable' control over the prethermal lifetime. This work establishes a powerful theoretical tool for stabilizing non-equilibrium quantum states.
main_problem: The paper addresses the conflict between linear stability analysis, which suggests trajectories remain near stable periodic orbits (SPOs), and thermodynamic principles, which predict eventual Floquet heating in periodically driven many-body systems.
main_result: They demonstrate that a long-lived prethermal regime exists, whose lifetime can be controlled by engineering the emergent quasiparticle band structure to achieve a 'doubly tunable' parametric dependence ($	au_{	ext{pre}} \propto R^{-W}$).
method: The analysis involves linearizing dynamics around SPOs to obtain an effective quasiparticle band structure and then deriving the scaling of the prethermal lifetime by analyzing time-averaged excitation rate equations.
model_or_system: The study uses a periodically driven (Floquet) spin system, specifically modeled as a 2D classical Ising system on a square lattice with nearest-neighbor and further-range couplings. The dynamics are governed by the periodicity $H(t) = H(t+T)$.
key_observables: Prethermal lifetime ($	au_{	ext{pre}}$), quasiparticle momentum space width ($R$), and the dispersion exponent ($W$).
important_parameters: The driving period $T$, coupling constants ($J, g$), and the engineered coefficients ($c_m$) that determine the band structure.
main_assumptions: Key assumptions include describing perturbations via an effective quasiparticle band structure and assuming the quasiparticle distribution remains close to its initial Gaussian form for the scaling derivation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate spin dynamics following SPOs, stability diagrams showing stable regions away from high-frequency limits, and plots comparing initial versus time-evolved quasiparticle momentum distributions at varying exponents $W$.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical model and the tension between linear stability and heating. It then uses PO construction and linear analysis to find a gapless dispersion relation. Finally, it derives the scaling law $	au \propto R^{-W}$ by analyzing excitation rates and shows how further-range interactions allow for engineering $W$.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete mechanism—band structure engineering—to stabilize non-equilibrium quantum phases in driven systems, bridging concepts from classical nonlinear dynamics (periodic orbits) to many-body chaos.
